items.headline: Energy bills rise again, with winter help left to Wednesday’s Budget
items.standfirst: Ofgem’s price cap rose 4% to £1,723 on 1 October, and only electricity got a VAT cut. Whether the Chancellor adds help on 28 October is unannounced; Ofgem sets the January cap by 25 November.

items.headline: Retail sales fall and confidence sinks a week before the Budget
items.standfirst: Retail volumes fell 0.4% in September, more than forecast, and a GfK survey put consumer confidence at its lowest since April. The Bank of England, which decides on rates on 5 November, had said energy prices were not yet weighing on dem…

items.headline: Fraud is now nearly half of crime in England and Wales
items.standfirst: By number of incidents, fraud made up 46% of crime in the year to June, and it rose 11% while the total held flat, the Office for National Statistics says. Police records show shoplifting and knife crime falling, but part of that is reco…

items.headline: UN says the world will overshoot 1.5°C, as COP31 nears
items.standfirst: The UN Environment Programme’s annual report says the 1.5°C limit can no longer be held without a period above it. National pledges would deliver 5–8% emissions cuts by 2030; its best remaining path needs 18%.

items.headline: UK borrowing runs £6bn over forecast as the Budget nears
items.standfirst: Public debt passed £3 trillion in September and debt interest hit a record for the month, the Office for National Statistics says. A £4bn downward revision to earlier months narrowed the overshoot; economists still put the Chancellor’s r…

items.headline: Fuel lifts UK inflation to 3.5%, making a November rate rise likelier
items.standfirst: Petrol and diesel drove September’s jump from 3.1%, the Office for National Statistics says, but services inflation also rose to 3.7%, the sign the Bank of England is watching. It decides on 5 November, a week after the Budget.

items.headline: Bank of England edges towards a rate rise on 5 November
items.standfirst: Three of nine rate-setters voted in September to raise Bank Rate to 4%, and three of those who held have since signalled they may join them. The case rests on an energy shock that, so far, has not spread into pay.

items.headline: Two official UK jobs counts have drifted almost half a million apart
items.standfirst: The Labour Force Survey shows 356,000 more people in work than a year ago; payrolls show 111,000 fewer employees. Unemployment fell to 4.7%, but the ONS says to read the sources together.

items.headline: Burnham pivots to youth jobs, but most NEETs are not looking for work
items.standfirst: The prime minister says benefits should be a “backstop” for the 981,000 young people outside work and education. Three in five of them are not job-hunting, and the schemes costed so far reach thousands a year.

items.headline: Burnham’s triple lock change will not pay for free care soon, IFS says
items.standfirst: The prime minister says dropping the pension’s annual earnings link from 2030 would save £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s. The Institute for Fiscal Studies expects about £4bn by the mid-2030s, and says it could be nothing.

items.headline: Asylum appeal waits reach 72 weeks as MPs weigh replacing tribunal judges
items.standfirst: Ministry of Justice figures show 156,000 appeals open in June, 90,000 of them asylum. Yet new appeals fell 21% in a year, and the new authority would not hear cases until late 2027.

items.headline: IFS: spending pressures, not headroom, are Healey’s main Budget challenge
items.standfirst: The Institute for Fiscal Studies puts headroom on the Chancellor’s main fiscal rule at about £20bn, against £24bn in March. The bigger problem, it says, is departmental budgets that higher inflation is eroding.

items.headline: Visas for overseas care workers have all but stopped
items.standfirst: The Home Office granted 344 care-worker visas to people applying from abroad in the year to June 2026, against 107,772 in 2023. Providers can still sponsor migrants already in the UK, but only until July 2028.

items.headline: Multi-cancer blood test did not cut late-stage cancers in NHS trial
items.standfirst: Across 142,250 adults in England, three yearly rounds of GRAIL’s Galleri test did not lower stage III and IV cancers, the trial’s main goal. Stage IV cases were 14% lower, but whether lives are saved will take years to show.

items.headline: Study visa falls now come from students, not their families
items.standfirst: The Home Office granted 383,455 study visas in the year to June 2026, 41% below the 2023 peak; students' own visas fell 12%. English universities, reliant on overseas fees for nearly a quarter of income, face a levy from 2028.

items.headline: UK electric car sales are closing on the mandate target, slowly
items.standfirst: Battery electric cars took 26.2% of new UK sales in January to September, against 20.2% a year earlier and a 33% target for 2026. Government figures show the mandate's flexibilities added about seven points to the effective share in 2025.

items.headline: UK growth slowed to 0.1% in August as services stalled
items.standfirst: The Office for National Statistics says GDP rose 0.1% in August after 0.4% in each of June and July, even as the three months to August grew 0.7%. Services, which drove that quarterly gain, showed no growth in the month.

items.headline: UK rainfall looked normal in September, but England was a third short
items.standfirst: The Met Office puts UK rainfall for September at 104% of average, while England received 65%. The Environment Agency says 11 areas of England are in drought and reservoirs are 54% full.

items.headline: Finland's unemployment rate now matches Spain's
items.standfirst: Eurostat's figures for August put Finland at 9.9% and Spain at 10.0%, the two highest in the euro area. In 2013 Spain's annual average was 17.8 percentage points higher.

items.headline: Prison numbers are flat since 2015, but recalls have nearly doubled
items.standfirst: England and Wales held 85,858 prisoners on 30 June 2026, almost exactly as many as in June 2015, but nearly twice as many were there on recall. Fewer people are serving ordinary sentences, and more are on remand.

items.headline: World food prices reach their highest since 2022 on grain and sugar
items.standfirst: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's price index averaged 136.0 in September, 5.8% above a year earlier and level with November 2022. Cereals rose 17% over the year and dairy fell 19%, and a US report on 9 October undercut one reas…

items.headline: Long NHS waits offset about 4% of treatment's fall in benefit claims
items.standfirst: The Office for National Statistics estimates that waits above 2015–16 levels are linked to up to 60,572 extra years of benefit receipt among treated inpatients. Set against what treatment is linked to, that is a small share, and more tha…

items.headline: Most suicides registered in 2025 happened in earlier years
items.standfirst: Of 6,162 suicides registered in England and Wales in 2025, 2,533 happened that year, according to the Office for National Statistics. That share has held near 40% for three years, so trends compare fairly, but a single year's change is h…

items.headline: About one in six English five-year-olds lacks a second MMR dose
items.standfirst: The UK Health Security Agency's annual childhood vaccination report puts two-dose MMR coverage at 83.8% for five-year-olds in England in 2025-26, below its 87.6% peak. Laboratory-confirmed measles cases rose to 390 in January to March.

items.headline: Farmland specialist birds have lost three-quarters of their numbers since 1970
items.standfirst: Defra's annual wild bird statistics, updated on 13 October, put the UK's farmland specialists 75% below their 1970 level, three times the fall for farmland generalists. The headline index for all breeding birds is down only 19%, because…

items.headline: Concentration has fallen in the UK's biggest industries, not the typical one
items.standfirst: The Office for National Statistics says the top five firms' share of turnover fell from 45% to 38% between 2010 and 2025, weighted by industry turnover. Across industries counted equally, it is unchanged at 47%.

items.headline: England's wildfire count through August is second only to 2022
items.standfirst: Fire services in England attended 1,354 wildfires from January to August 2026, provisional figures show. That is 2.5 times the average for the same months in 2011–2025, and nine in ten came in July and August.

items.headline: England's 18-week waiting performance has held near 65% since March
items.standfirst: In August, 65.2% of patients on England's NHS waiting list had waited up to 18 weeks, 4.2 points better than a year earlier. Most of that gain came in a single month, and the share has barely moved since.

items.headline: Police records and a survey disagree on who faces more religious hate crime
items.standfirst: Police in England and Wales recorded 117 religious hate crimes per 10,000 Jewish residents and 13 per 10,000 Muslims in the year to March 2026. The Crime Survey, which asks people directly, estimates that more Muslims than Jewish people…

items.headline: UK growth was second-fastest in the G7 this spring, after a 2025 in which two quarters recorded none
items.standfirst: The ONS now puts April to June 2026 growth at 0.5%, behind only Canada. Revisions in the same release moved 2025 around: the second and fourth quarters came out at 0.0%, so the 2026 pickup follows a stall.

items.headline: A new ONS method halves the size of Britain's productivity slowdown since 2009
items.standfirst: Counting hours worked from several sources, rather than one household survey, lifts estimated output-per-hour growth for 2009 to 2019 from 0.7% a year to 1.3%. The figures are indicative and not yet official, and the ONS plans to adopt t…

items.headline: Fewer than one in ten UK adults now smoke, but the rate is five times higher without qualifications
items.standfirst: Smoking has fallen from 20.2% of adults in 2011 to 9.8% in 2025, a drop of more than half. The fall has been steepest among the young. The gap between the least and most qualified has not closed.

items.headline: Emissions rose in 2025, but the yearly rise in the air's carbon dioxide fell by a third
items.standfirst: Fossil-fuel emissions rose again last year, yet NOAA's Mauna Loa record shows the annual increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide dropped from 3.33 to 2.23 parts per million, and 2026 is running slower still. The Global Carbon Budget puts…

items.headline: Fewer than four in ten asylum claims now succeed at first decision, half the 2022 peak
items.standfirst: The Home Office granted protection in 38% of initial decisions in the year to June 2026, down from 48% a year earlier and 77% at the 2022 peak. The biggest single shift is Syria. The rate is for first decisions only, and appeals have his…

items.headline: UK borrowing is below last year's pace but £8.1bn above forecast, with benefits the biggest spending rise
items.standfirst: Five months into the financial year, the government has borrowed £2.2bn less than a year ago but £8.1bn more than the Office for Budget Responsibility expected. Higher benefits, not debt interest, account for the largest part of the extr…

items.headline: Britain’s hottest summer on record broke a record set only a year earlier
items.standfirst: Summer 2026 averaged 16.5°C across the UK, the highest in a series that starts in 1884 and 0.4°C above the record 2025 set. Seven of the ten hottest summers have come since 2000, and the warmth carried on into a joint-fourth-warmest Sept…

items.headline: Britain has 2.5 unemployed people for every vacancy, the most outside the pandemic since 2015
items.standfirst: Vacancies have fallen to 702,000 while the number of unemployed people has risen, so each job opening now has more people chasing it than at any point in a decade. The ratio has stopped climbing, but it has not come back down.

items.headline: The world’s oceans have set a temperature record four months running, NOAA data show
items.standfirst: With El Niño conditions in the Pacific, every month from June to September 2026 was the warmest on record for global sea surfaces in NOAA’s dataset — and September was the second-warmest September for the planet as a whole.

items.headline: Three in ten UK businesses now use AI, more than triple the share in 2023
items.standfirst: Official survey data show adoption climbing fastest in large firms and in tech. Where AI-using firms report any effect on staff numbers, cuts outnumber hires — but most report no change at all.

items.headline: Covid-19 has dropped out of the world’s ten leading causes of death. Dementia is now fifth
items.standfirst: New World Health Organization estimates for 2023 show the pandemic’s direct death toll falling by nine-tenths in two years, while the diseases of ageing — heart disease, stroke, dementia, diabetes — tighten their hold.

items.headline: Arctic summer sea ice has stalled for two decades — at levels lower than any year before 2007
items.standfirst: This year's Arctic minimum tied for the tenth-lowest on record. The 20 years since 2007 hold the 20 lowest minimums, yet the minimum has shown no significant decline across them — a slowdown scientists are still trying to explain.

items.headline: The ocean surface ran further above normal in September than in any month on NOAA's 177-year record
items.standfirst: NOAA puts September's global sea surface temperature 1.10°C above its 20th-century average. That beats August's record, but only by 0.02°C, with El Niño conditions persisting in the Pacific.

items.headline: Small-boat arrivals are down by two-fifths this year, but each boat is carrying a record load
items.standfirst: Home Office figures show 42% fewer people and 49% fewer boats crossing the Channel than at the same point in 2025. Boats have kept getting fuller, averaging 67 people this year.

items.headline: UK population growth slows to its weakest since 2020 as net migration falls by two-thirds
items.standfirst: The UK grew by 227,700 people in the year to mid-2025. Almost all of that came from migration, because births outnumbered deaths by just 4,900.

items.headline: Recorded ship transits through the Strait of Hormuz are running 96% below their 2025 average
items.standfirst: IMF satellite tracking counted an average of 3.6 ships a day through the strait in September, against 85.5 a day across 2025. Seven months after Iran's Revolutionary Guards declared it closed, traffic has recovered once, for less than fo…

items.headline: Indonesia's fires are burning at close to 2015's pace, but have not yet matched its carbon
items.standfirst: By 11 September Indonesia's fires had released 76.2 megatonnes of carbon this year, according to Copernicus satellite estimates. That is behind the catastrophic 2015 season at the same point, and about two-fifths of 2019's total. The sea…

items.headline: This El Niño is second only to 1997 for the time of year — and still short of the four biggest
items.standfirst: NOAA's official index put July–September 2026 at +1.69°C, the second-highest reading for that season since 1950. All four El Niños that went on to peak above +2.0°C were still building at this stage. Whether 2026 joins them is, for now,…

items.headline: Britain’s pension system relies on more than the state
items.standfirst: A comparison with the G7, the Netherlands and Australia shows why state pension payments alone cannot tell us how well a retirement system works.

items.headline: Anaesthesia study finds shared neural changes across six species
items.standfirst: A peer-reviewed comparison identifies a common subset of changes in neural activity. The findings concern information processing and responsiveness, with limits on what they reveal about consciousness.

items.headline: WHO records more cholera deaths despite fewer reported cases
items.standfirst: Reported cases fell in 2025 while deaths rose. The divergence highlights why a smaller surveillance total cannot, on its own, establish progress.

items.headline: Healthy ageing policies expand, but tracking remains limited
items.standfirst: WHO’s midpoint update shows wider policy coverage for older people. Measuring whether those policies improve lives remains a separate challenge.

items.headline: Innovation rankings hide different routes to results
items.standfirst: WIPO’s 2026 index separates the conditions for innovation from its measured outputs. The scores reveal contrasts that a single league table conceals, but cannot establish which economy gets the best return on investment.

items.headline: Ageing doctors, unequal staffing: two pressures on health care
items.standfirst: WHO’s latest workforce findings show a wide Europe–Africa staffing gap. Older doctor workforces and uneven local coverage add different challenges for health services.

items.headline: When neighbours vanish, glassfish pull away
items.standfirst: A Nature study finds that disappearing virtual neighbours can prompt retreat — but their swimming must first look natural.

items.headline: In four months, Bundibugyo Ebola has recorded more than twice the cases of DR Congo's largest previous outbreak
items.standfirst: DR Congo has confirmed 7,890 cases and 3,799 deaths since 15 May, against 3,470 cases and 2,287 deaths in the whole two-year Kivu epidemic of 2018-20. New cases have stopped accelerating, but they have not yet begun to fall.

items.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% as energy costs jump
items.standfirst: The Consumer Prices Index rose to 3.1% in the year to August 2026, up from 2.9% in July, as motor fuel and domestic energy prices climbed faster than the rest of the household basket, official data show.

items.headline: The Atlantic has gone longer without a hurricane than in any season since 1914
items.standfirst: Six named storms, no hurricanes: 2026 has passed the satellite-era record for the latest first hurricane by 13 days, and storm energy is running at 8% of normal for the date.

items.headline: By land, Rome was not the hub of its empire’s road network
items.standfirst: A network analysis of 299,171 km of Roman roads finds Antioch, Ancyra, Byzantium and Corinth were better-placed overland crossroads than Rome, while 35 of 45 provincial capitals ranked in their province’s top tenth on at least one centra…

items.headline: Democrats need three House seats and four in the Senate — and the White House party has lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms
items.standfirst: Americans vote on 3 November for every House seat and about a third of the Senate. Here is the arithmetic, the historical record, and what forecasters and betting markets make of the four ways control of Congress could land — including w…

items.headline: Britain's winter averages show no trace of El Niño. February does
items.standfirst: Across 76 winters since 1951, El Niño strength tracks neither UK winter temperature nor UK winter rainfall. But of the nine strongest El Niño winters, six ended February with the blocked, colder circulation that steers Atlantic storms aw…

items.headline: Multivitamins and immunity: the biggest trials find no effect, in healthy and immunosuppressed people alike
items.standfirst: Randomised evidence covering more than 64,000 people finds little sign that broad-spectrum supplements prevent coughs, colds or infections. Where supplementation clearly works, it is a single nutrient correcting a documented shortfall —…

items.headline: More adults have never married, and most of them do not live with a partner either
items.standfirst: New ONS figures for England and Wales show 34.9% of adults have never married or formed a civil partnership, up from 32.6% ten years ago. The usual assumption is that they are living together instead. Most are not.

items.headline: NOAA changed how it measures El Niño — at this stage, that moves 2026 from first place to fourth
items.standfirst: Measured against a fixed 30-year average, the central Pacific has just had its warmest May–July since 1950. Measured against the rest of the tropical ocean — NOAA's official method since February — three past El Niños were warmer at the…

items.headline: Paracetamol showed no effect during pregnancy — and an impossible one before it
items.standfirst: Children exposed in the womb were no more likely to be diagnosed with autism or ADHD than their own brothers and sisters. But the same records showed a raised risk among mothers who took paracetamol before they conceived — pills that nev…

items.headline: Bookmakers price Count Binface near 10/1 in Clacton. Polymarket prices him at 1%.
items.standfirst: Fixed-odds firms and the largest prediction market differ by close to a factor of ten on Nigel Farage's satirical challenger, while agreeing almost exactly on Farage. The only poll of Clacton voters puts Binface 53 points behind.

items.headline: Totality lasts longest where almost nobody lives
items.standfirst: An estimated 15.2 million residents lie inside the path of the 12 August total solar eclipse. Nearly all of them are in Spain, at the end of the track, where the eclipsed Sun sits low over the horizon and no place gets two full minutes.

items.headline: AI models sorted fictional ethnic groups into job types more sharply than people did
items.standfirst: A peer-reviewed study ran 16 language models through a 40-round hiring game in which four made-up demographic groups were equally likely to succeed at everything. Frontier models funnelled the groups into particular job types at 1.39 on…

items.headline: Current polls imply a more fragmented party system than any postwar election
items.standfirst: The effective number of parties implied by early-August voting-intention polls is between 5.2 and 5.6. At the 2024 general election, the postwar record, it was 4.70; in 1951 it was 2.14. Polls measure stated intention, not votes cast.

items.headline: Four episodes of interbreeding — and two partners no one has ever sequenced
items.standfirst: A new method reads ancient interbreeding out of the DNA of living people alone, with no archaic genome to compare against. It recovers the known Neanderthal and Denisovan signals, and finds two more — from lineages that have no fossil, n…

items.headline: How 235 earthworks become three million people
items.standfirst: A laser survey of 4,497 square kilometres of Amazonian rainforest documented 432 earthworks, 396 of them previously unknown. Turning that into a peak population of 1.25 to 3 million takes five multiplications — and the last one can move…

items.headline: Taiwan screened 57,065 laser leads to find one tree. The laser still read it low.
items.standfirst: Airborne LiDAR flagged tens of thousands of possible giants across Taiwan, most of them ordinary trees perched on cliffs. Volunteers discarded nine in ten. On the giants that survived the filter, the model's remaining error mostly ran th…

items.headline: Ten years of solar-storm forecasts have moved the arrival-time error by 1.2 hours
items.standfirst: Across 1,702 logged predictions of when a coronal mass ejection would reach Earth, the average miss is 13.2 hours. The scoreboard's first five years averaged 14.0; the five and a half years since, 12.8.

items.headline: Scientists propose ocean oxygen loss as a new planetary boundary
items.standfirst: A peer-reviewed review argues aquatic deoxygenation belongs alongside climate change and biodiversity loss on the list of processes that keep Earth liveable. The open ocean has already lost more than 2% of its oxygen since 1960, mostly o…

items.headline: EU AI Act enforcement begins — but its toughest rules are delayed 16 months
items.standfirst: Fines for general-purpose AI models and new transparency duties became enforceable across the EU this week. The high-risk system rules meant to be the Act's centrepiece won't apply until December 2027.

items.headline: Long-term sickness is the single biggest reason 9.1 million people are economically inactive
items.standfirst: Long-term sickness, studying, caring for family and retirement between them account for around six in seven of the UK's 9.1 million economically inactive 16- to 64-year-olds. Long-term sickness is now the largest single reason, though bo…

items.headline: Fish and chips has risen more than twice as fast as inflation since 2019
items.standfirst: A portion of fish and chips now costs 72% more than in July 2019 — more than double the rise in overall prices, and in the cost of fish itself, official figures show.

items.headline: Births in England and Wales fall to a 1977-level low — and the data can't yet say why
items.standfirst: 585,396 babies were born in 2025, the fewest in any year since 1977 and a fourth straight fall in the fertility rate. Whether today's twentysomethings are delaying parenthood or forgoing it is still unknown — and the answer matters for h…

items.headline: States building the most data centres have had the smallest electricity price rises
items.standfirst: A causal study finds data-centre growth pushed the average U.S. residential electricity rate down between 2019 and 2024. But in the grid serving Virginia's "Data Center Alley," the effect runs the other way — and researchers warn the nat…

items.headline: EU wildfires: burnt area is running at two and a half times the 20-year average
items.standfirst: Fires have burnt 434,976 hectares across the EU by 29 July, more than during the same point in 2025 — itself the worst full season on record. But how bad the picture looks depends on whose count is used: national tallies run lower than E…

items.headline: Britain has had the G7's highest ten-year borrowing cost for 23 months running
items.standfirst: The gap between UK and German ten-year yields reached 2.26 points in December 2024 — wider than in the month after the mini-budget — and has not returned to its pre-2022 range since. On the IMF's projections of debt and deficit, Britain…

items.headline: Bundibugyo Ebola is outpacing the 2014 and 2018 epidemics, with no vaccine matched to it
items.standfirst: Seventy-two days after the outbreak was declared, DR Congo had reported 3,262 confirmed cases. At a comparable point the 2018 North Kivu outbreak had reported 223 — and responders there had a matching vaccine within a week.

items.headline: After 35 years of warming, "stable" soil carbon starts to break down too
items.standfirst: A Massachusetts forest plot has been artificially warmed by 5°C for decades. A new peer-reviewed analysis finds that even its most chemically stable soil carbon, once assumed safe from decomposition, began breaking down during the trial'…

items.headline: A new method removes 99.99% of PFOS from water. It releases 35% of the fluorine.
items.standfirst: Two German studies report genuine breakdown of a “forever chemical”, not just capture. But the measure that shows carbon–fluorine bonds actually breaking lags far behind the removal figure — and in the best-performing runs, most of the f…

items.headline: Britain's stated interest in news has almost halved since 2015
items.standfirst: In 2015, 70% of UK respondents to the Reuters Institute's annual survey called themselves extremely or very interested in news. This year it is 37% — the second-largest fall of the ten markets the report compares on a 2015 baseline, and…

items.headline: Three in four of the NCSC’s critical-infrastructure cases are now believed to be state-linked
items.standfirst: The agency’s total caseload has been flat across two reporting years while the tier it rates nationally significant more than tripled. Officials describe the capability that matters as patience — years of quiet access through known, unpa…

items.headline: Britons trust scientists at 81% — but worldwide, people underestimate each other's willingness to act by 26 points
items.standfirst: Public trust in science has not collapsed; the survey record is clear on that. But trust is not transmission. In all 125 countries measured, people badly misjudge what their neighbours think — and what circulates online is selected for n…

items.headline: Koala populations began collapsing 100,000 years ago — long before humans reached Australia
items.standfirst: A newly calibrated genomic mutation clock shows koala numbers falling to about a tenth of their peak roughly 100,000 years ago, tens of thousands of years before humans are thought to have set foot on the continent.

items.headline: Stanford's 'natural Ozempic' peptide cut animal appetite in half — no human has taken it yet
items.standfirst: BRP, an AI-discovered peptide, suppressed appetite in mice and pigs without the nausea common to GLP-1 drugs. The Nature study is 16 months old, and no human trial has begun.

items.headline: UK youth unemployment hits 16.4%, an 11-year high
items.standfirst: The unemployment rate for 16-to-24-year-olds rose to its highest level since 2014 in the three months to May, as UK job vacancies fell to a five-year low.

items.headline: Civilian killings in conflict hit their highest level since 1994
items.standfirst: Global deaths in organised conflict reached 244,600 in 2025, the second-worst toll since the Rwandan genocide, new data shows. Battlefield deaths barely moved — the rise came almost entirely from a 438% jump in the deliberate killing of…

items.headline: Ordinary streetlights are pulling thousands of woodlice into synchronised, circling "mills"
items.standfirst: A newly documented isopod species has been filmed forming mass, night-time circles under artificial light in northern Israel — a behaviour never recorded in woodlice before, on evidence from just five nights.

items.headline: The Sun contains 55% more silver than previously calculated
items.standfirst: A new 3D non-LTE model of the Sun's atmosphere finds far more silver than the standard reference value assumed, closing most of a long-standing mismatch with primitive meteorites — though a small gap remains.

items.headline: Britain's two main parties just posted their worst combined result since 1918
items.standfirst: Labour and the Conservatives won a combined 57.4% of the vote at the 2024 election, the lowest share since the franchise was widened to near-universal suffrage. National polling since the election puts the two parties even lower, with Re…

items.headline: One in seven adults have used AI instead of seeing a GP
items.standfirst: Polling for King's College London finds convenience and curiosity outrank NHS waiting times as the reason people turn to a chatbot over a doctor, and one in five of those who have say it talked them out of seeing a professional.

items.headline: 42% of UK adults are deliberately limiting their use of AI
items.standfirst: The top reason is privacy and security, not confusion. Just 6% of those cutting back say they feel unprepared to use the technology.

items.headline: UK inflation has fallen back below its pre-conflict level, despite the Middle East fuel shock
items.standfirst: The war between Israel, the US and Iran added three tenths of a point to UK inflation in a single month as pump prices spiked. Four months on, headline CPI is lower than before the conflict began, even though the Bank of England's own fo…

items.headline: US tariffs on 60 economies take effect under a law with no expiry date
items.standfirst: A 10-12.5% tariff on imports from 60 countries and the EU, including a 10% rate for the UK, took effect on 24 July under a statute with no legislated end - succeeding an emergency levy that expired, by law, the same day.

items.headline: Britain's ten commonest pub names are all shrinking - and in almost perfect lockstep
items.standfirst: Measured on one consistent database five years apart, every one of the ten most common pub names lost pubs, at rates clustered between 4.5% and 9.6%. Seven of the ten held their exact rank. Pub names aren't dying off one by one - the who…

items.headline: Sequels and franchise films now dominate the UK box-office top 10
items.standfirst: In 2000, one in five of the UK's ten biggest films at the cinema were sequels, remakes or franchise entries. By 2025 the figure was nine in ten, the steepest climb across the years Noodle News surveyed since 1989.

items.headline: Two cables carry most of Britain's transatlantic data — and both come ashore in Cornwall
items.standfirst: Nine of the roughly 64 subsea cables reaching UK shores land at a single beach in Cornwall, and just two of them carry three-quarters of Great Britain's transatlantic data capacity. Parliament's security committee calls that clustering a…

items.headline: Aviva beat the market by 11 points. It did not beat its own sector.
items.standfirst: Between its 5 June low and 24 July the insurer returned 14.6% against a FTSE 100 up 3.6%. Over the five weeks in which its sector index can be measured alongside it, Aviva lagged that index. The gap is a benchmark artefact, not company n…

items.headline: Cash bounced back for a single year. Then its decline resumed.
items.standfirst: In 2022 the number of cash payments in the UK rose for the first time in a decade, as households turned to notes and coins to budget through the cost-of-living squeeze. The rebound proved a one-year exception: by 2024 cash had fallen to…

items.headline: UK crime profilers read the scene well. They rarely name the suspect
items.standfirst: A study of the National Crime Agency's behavioural profiling unit finds it usefully illuminates a crime scene in 95% of reports, but adds a genuinely new line of enquiry in only 40%. The method's most notorious UK case shows what happens…

items.headline: Antarctic sea ice's slow climb broke in 2016 — and the record book keeps being rewritten
items.standfirst: For three decades Antarctic sea ice drifted gently upward. Since 2016 its winter peak and summer low have repeatedly hit the lowest levels in the 47-year satellite record, though 2026 shows the first sign the run may be easing.

items.headline: Nearly a quarter of low- and middle-income countries now spend over a fifth of revenue on interest alone
items.standfirst: Interest payments by low- and middle-income countries have more than doubled since 2017 as a share of government revenue. The causes are contested; the arithmetic of what that leaves for health, education and infrastructure is not.

items.headline: Return-to-office mandates have not been shown to improve business performance
items.standfirst: Randomised trials find that two days a week at home costs nothing in measured output and cuts quitting by about a third. The largest study of corporate mandates found no gain in profit or firm value. But the evidence does show one real c…

items.headline: ONS now publishes two versions of UK productivity for the same quarter — and they disagree on the sign
items.standfirst: For the same three months, one official measure of output per hour shows a fall and another shows a rise. The gap says less about the economy than about how unsettled the underlying survey still is.

items.headline: England's NHS waiting list is down from its peak, but still 93% bigger than a decade ago
items.standfirst: The list has fallen from its record 7.77 million in September 2023 to 7.2 million. But that is still far above 2017 levels, and how long people wait now varies sharply by specialty.

items.headline: UK rents hit a record high — but the boom that drove them there is over
items.standfirst: Average UK private rent reached £1,383 a month in May 2026. But annual rent inflation has fallen from a record 9.1% two years ago to 3.3% today, and the regions that drove the surge have swapped places with the ones that once lagged.

items.headline: Company insolvencies have plateaued at a 30-year high since 2023
items.standfirst: England and Wales have recorded around 24,000 company insolvencies a year since 2023 — the highest sustained level in three decades — but the total has stopped climbing, and H1 2026 ran 7% below H1 2025. Age data shows established busine…

items.headline: AI's proven wins are real but narrow — broad payoff is still rare
items.standfirst: Controlled trials show genuine gains from AI in specific, well-defined tasks: customer support, cancer screening, narrow coding jobs. But national data show only a fifth of US firms use it day to day, and most companies still can't show…

items.headline: Renewables closed on coal in the world's electricity mix in 2025 — and by one tracker's count, moved ahead
items.standfirst: Two independent trackers agree that renewables and coal converged to roughly a third of global electricity generation each in 2025. Ember's count puts renewables narrowly in front for the first time in over a century; the IEA's independe…

items.headline: Britain's life expectancy stall is real — and it's the worst in Europe
items.standfirst: ONS life tables confirm UK gains in life expectancy have flatlined since around 2011. A 20-country study finds the slowdown wasn't unique to Britain — but no other country's was as sharp.

items.headline: Resistant infections in England rose 9% in a year. The world added four new antibiotics in two.
items.standfirst: UKHSA recorded 20,484 antibiotic-resistant bloodstream infections in England in 2024. WHO's global pipeline review found 90 antibacterial drugs in development worldwide, but only a handful target the bacteria it ranks most dangerous, and…

items.headline: Two-thirds of households in the deepest food insecurity never used a food bank
items.standfirst: Trussell's parcel count fell 12% in 2025. A separate government household survey shows why parcel counts and the true scale of food insecurity tell different stories.

items.headline: No English council has gone bankrupt over its budget in two and a half years
items.standfirst: Section 114 notices, the closest thing to municipal bankruptcy, piled up between 2018 and 2023, then stopped. What changed was not council finances: a record £1.5bn in emergency government support for 2026/27 alone is bridging the gap, a…

items.headline: The World's Fertility Rate Has Been Cut by More Than Half Since the 1950s, and the Age Balance Is Already Shifting
items.standfirst: Global births per woman have fallen from about 4.9 in the 1950s to 2.25 today, and 55% of countries are already below the replacement level. The workforce-to-retiree shift this produces is not a future scenario in the OECD area — it is a…

items.headline: Four-day week evidence: a government trial and a campaign-run trial, compared
items.standfirst: Iceland's 2015-2019 hours cut was run and evaluated by the public employers themselves. The UK's widely cited 2022 pilot was organised by the campaign for the policy, using companies that volunteered. Both found gains, but the two eviden…

items.headline: Air-to-Water Machines Are Scaling — Just Not Into City Taps
items.standfirst: Atmospheric water generators are moving out of disaster kits and into schools, hospitals and refugee camps worldwide. But the economics still keep them roughly 100 times pricier than tap water, per litre — a gap that keeps the technology…

items.headline: Orbit got 96% cheaper. The industries built on that are mostly still on paper
items.standfirst: Launching a kilogram to orbit costs 96% less than in 1960, and forecasters expect it to keep falling. That collapse is real and measured. But satellite refuelling, asteroid mining and orbital data centres — the industries the cheap launc…

items.headline: US digital nomads pass 18.5 million, but no one agrees how many exist worldwide
items.standfirst: A consistent seven-year survey series puts America's digital-nomad workforce at 18.5 million and growing. Beyond the US border, published estimates of the same population differ by a factor of two or more.

items.headline: Cinema's Capital Went to Television. Now Both Are Shrinking.
items.standfirst: Since 2002, US and Canadian cinema admissions have fallen by more than half. Since 2022, the number of scripted TV series has fallen too. Thirty years of data show money leaving the multiplex for prestige television — then leaving much o…

items.headline: London's escape to the country has gone into reverse
items.standfirst: Londoners bought 57,660 homes outside the capital in 2025 — down 44% from the 2021 pandemic peak of 103,310, and below the pre-pandemic average. Faster house-price growth outside London and tightening office-attendance rules, not a colla…

items.headline: DNA reading costs fell 782 times further than writing costs. A silicon chip has now written 64 strands in water.
items.standfirst: A Harvard-led team used a CMOS chip to synthesise 64 distinct DNA sequences at once, enzymatically, in water — the largest published parallel enzymatic demonstration. Placed on two decades of cost data, it is a laboratory first. No cost…

items.headline: The heat was measured to two decimal places. The death toll is two different numbers.
items.standfirst: Western Europe averaged 20.74°C in June — a record, and 3.06°C above normal. For the single week the heat peaked, Europe has two figures for the dead: 10,650 and 20,390. One starts from registered deaths. The other never looks at one.

items.headline: Chimpanzees chose the crystal. The 780,000-year anchor belongs to a site the study never cites.
items.standfirst: Nine rescued chimpanzees near Madrid picked quartz and calcite out of pebble piles within seconds, then held them up to the light for minutes at a time. That much is measured. The claim that it explains 780,000 years of human mineral-col…

items.headline: England's measles jab rate is rising on average. In the poorest areas it is falling.
items.standfirst: The national second-dose figure has gone up for three quarters running. In the latest quarter, coverage in the 30 most deprived councils fell — and the gap to the least deprived reached 10.6 points, the widest of the four childhood vacci…

items.headline: Eleven times, a lab has made more fusion energy than its lasers delivered
items.standfirst: Since December 2022 the National Ignition Facility has reached fusion ignition eleven times, peaking at a record 8.6 megajoules in April 2025. But that milestone counts energy on target — not the roughly 300–400 megajoules the lasers dra…

items.headline: CRISPR’s cure is real and it is holding. Last year, 64 people received it.
items.standfirst: Nine in ten treated patients are free of the crises that defined their disease, and the effect has now lasted more than five years. Yet in the ten countries where the therapy is licensed, over 60,000 people are eligible — and 64 were inf…

items.headline: Frontier AI’s exam scores have stalled near the ceiling. Its real-world reach is still doubling.
items.standfirst: The benchmarks the industry leaned on have saturated, which makes progress look like a plateau. On task length — the least saturated measure available — the reach of frontier models has gone on doubling roughly every four to seven months…

items.headline: AI is still a small slice of the world’s electricity
items.standfirst: Data centres used about 1.5% of global electricity in 2024, and AI only a fraction of that. The load is growing fast and set to roughly double by 2030 — yet even then it would add less new demand than cooling or electric cars. The same p…

items.headline: Basic income barely moved how much people work. The cost is the sticking point.
items.standfirst: A decade of experiments — Helsinki, Texas, Stockton, rural Kenya — finds that unconditional cash reliably improves financial security and wellbeing, with small and mixed effects on employment. What none of them can settle is whether a co…

items.headline: The Burnham platform: where a new Labour leader would break from Starmer—and where he couldn’t
items.standfirst: Andy Burnham is the clear favourite to succeed Keir Starmer, who resigned on 22 June. He has no published manifesto, but in interviews he has set out positions that diverge from the present government on transport, public ownership, the…

items.headline: Money keeps buying happiness — just less of it with every step
items.standfirst: For most people, both day-to-day mood and overall life satisfaction keep climbing with income, and no study has yet found a ceiling. But the gains run through the logarithm of income, so each extra pound counts for less than the last. An…

items.headline: UK wages, the long view: stalled at home, lapped by the US
items.standfirst: Since the 2008 financial crisis, the average British wage has barely moved in real terms — up about 4% over fourteen years, while America’s rose four times as fast. The result is a typical pay packet still hovering around its 2008 level,…

items.headline: Net migration has nearly halved. But fewer people are choosing to come — not fewer arriving by boat.
items.standfirst: UK net migration fell to 171,000 in the year to December 2025 — its lowest in four years and 82% below the 2023 peak. The fall is driven almost entirely by fewer legal arrivals on work and study visas. Small boat crossings rose again in…

items.headline: Squeezed from both sides: why Keir Starmer became so unpopular
items.standfirst: A landslide built on a thin vote, a coalition pulling in opposite directions, and a run of named, datable decisions that tracked his ratings down. As reports swirl that the prime minister may set out his departure — unconfirmed by Downin…

items.headline: Britain leaned left and liberal. Its politics turned right anyway.
items.standfirst: The left–right spectrum can be measured — Britain has done it the same way since 1986. On those yardsticks the public's average economic and social attitudes have drifted left and become markedly more liberal over the past 15 years. Yet…

items.headline: Where do you sit on Britain's two value scales?
items.standfirst: The companion to our piece on the British spectrum. Answer the same eleven statements the British Social Attitudes survey has used since 1986 — five for the economic left–right scale, six for the liberal–authoritarian scale — and we'll p…

items.headline: Two years after a landslide, Keir Starmer’s leadership is in open crisis
items.standfirst: The Observer reports the prime minister is expected to set out a timetable for his departure on Monday; a government source told Reuters he remains focused on the job, and Downing Street has not confirmed anything. Whatever Monday brings…
